AE1/AE3, epithelial and T‑cell markers are negative, arguing against carcinoma or primary T/NK lymphoma.

- Extent of disease on FDG‑PET/CT (multifocal pulmonary/pleural, hepatic and very extensive osseous FDG‑avid lesions) strongly supports a systemic, high‑grade B‑cell lymphoma with extranodal dissemination.

- The clinical/laboratory constellation (prolonged fever, splenomegaly, bicytopenia affecting ≥2 lineages, marked hyperferritinemia, hypertriglyceridemia, hypofibrinogenemia, high transaminases) meets multiple HLH diagnostic criteria. Bone marrow may lack visible hemophagocytosis initially; absence of hemophagocytosis does not exclude HLH. Thus a secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (sHLH) triggered by an EBV‑positive B‑cell lymphoma is very likely and explains the severe cytopenias, coagulopathy markers, and hepatic dysfunction/jaundice.

- EBV DNA in blood is reported normal, but tissue EBER/LMP1 positivity demonstrates EBV involvement in the tumor cells; circulating viral load may be low or transient even when tissue is EBV‑driven. Post‑transplant/iatrogenic PTLD is another EBV‑driven B‑cell proliferative disorder that can be disseminated and provoke HLH if immunosuppression/transplant history is present. Primary EBV‑HLH (without overt lymphoma) can present very similarly biochemically but is less consistent with the biopsy demonstrating malignant B cells.

- Less likely: other high‑grade B‑cell lymphomas (plasmablastic lymphoma, high‑grade/Burkitt phenotypes) or Hodgkin lymphoma variants — immunophenotype and widespread osseous involvement make these less likely given the strong CD20/PAX5 and LMP1/EBER pattern.

The remaining differentials are other EBV‑associated B‑cell lymphoproliferative disorders (LYG, PTLD) or primary EBV‑HLH.
